以求稱
上意于時就試之士千餘人拔其尤者百人遵
定制也〔臣〕嘗竊思天之生才固俾為世用然

punctuated:
會試錄序

國朝受天明命，奄有萬邦。列聖相繼，所以承天心而固邦本者，莫先於養賢；其出而用之，則莫重於進士之科。得人之盛，致治之隆，自唐、虞、三代以來，莫有過焉者也。正統四年二月，行在禮部會試天下所貢士。尚書臣濙、侍郎臣士嘉以考試官為請，上命臣直、臣從善。其同考官則臣寬、臣一寧、臣益、臣復、臣孟𧦬、臣英、臣寔、臣潤生；監試則監察御史臣聰、臣慎；其諸執事皆遴選也。夙夜祗栗，以求稱上意。于時就試之士千餘人，拔其尤者百人，遵定制也。臣嘗竊思：天之生才，固俾為世用，然非人君養育而訓迪之，亦不能以成其才。
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Our Dynasty has received the bright mandate of Heaven and comprehensively possesses the myriad states. As the successive sacred Emperors have followed one another, in that whereby they uphold the mind of Heaven and consolidate the foundation of the state, nothing has taken precedence over nurturing the worthy; and when these worthies come forth and are employed, nothing is more important than the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) examination category. The flourishing of its recruitment of men of talent and the height of the good governance achieved have not been surpassed since the times of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties.

In the second month of the fourth year of the Zhengtong reign [1439], the Ministry of Rites at the Auxiliary Capital held the Metropolitan Examination for the tribute scholars presented from across the Empire. When Minister Your Servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙 and Vice Minister Your Servant [Wang] Shijia 王士嘉 petitioned for the appointment of Examiners, His Majesty commanded Your Servant [Wang] Zhi 王直 and Your Servant [Lan] Congshan 蘭從善 to serve. As for the Associate Examiners, they were Your Servant [Chen] Kuan 陳寬, Your Servant [Li] Yining 李一寧, Your Servant [Liu] Yi 劉益, Your Servant [Xu] Fu 許復, Your Servant [Wang] Mengjian 王孟𧦬, Your Servant [Wang] Ying 王英, Your Servant [Liu] Shi 劉寔, and Your Servant [Zhang] Runsheng 張潤生; as for the Supervisors of the Examination, they were Investigating Censors Your Servant Cong 聰 and Your Servant Shen 慎; and all the various functionaries were carefully selected. From morning till night we were reverent and trembling with awe, seeking to fulfill His Majesty's intentions. At this time, the scholars who sat for the examination numbered over a thousand, from whom we selected a hundred of the most outstanding, in compliance with the established system.

Your Servant has ventured to reflect quietly: when Heaven gives birth to men of talent, it assuredly causes them to be of use to the world; yet unless the ruler nurtures and instructs them, they still cannot bring their talents to completion…

潤澤日月之照臨霜雪之嚴沍然後長盛

translation_en:
This may be compared to great mountains and vast plateaus where timber grows: only after relying upon the moisture of rain and dew, the shining rays of the sun and moon, and the severe cold of frost and snow do the trees grow lush, firm, and dense. The large ones can serve as ridgepoles and beams, while the smaller ones are also sufficient to provide rafters—it simply depends on how they are used. Concerning the excellence of talented men in the flourishing Zhou dynasty, the poet sang in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing): "The royal state is able to produce them; they are the pillars of Zhou." And again: "Thus the grown men have virtue, and the young men have attainment." From this it can be seen.

With regard to worthy talents, the dynasty already nurtures them in schools. Scholars of the country lanes and villages, moved by His Majesty's virtue, likewise all rise up without exception, dedicating themselves to learning and inquiry, and coming to understand the principles of cultivating oneself and governing others. When they come forth to offer their service, all exhaust their talents in seeking to repay the throne. Now the realm has enjoyed great peace for nearly a hundred years; although this fundamentally stems from the supreme benevolence of the successive sacred emperors and the great virtue of the reigning Sovereign, the efficacy of nurturing talent is also evident herein. Having encountered an enlightened age and succeeded in being chosen in this selection, the day is soon coming when the candidates will advance to respond to the Emperor's personal inquiries at the Palace Examination and receive His glorious favor. 第壹塲

四書
學如不及，猶恐失之。
故為政在人，取人以身，修身以道，修道以仁。
無為其所不為，無欲其所不欲，如此而已矣。

易
乾元用九，乃見天則。
九五，有孚惠心，勿問元吉；有孚惠我德。象曰：有孚惠心，勿問之矣；惠我德，大得志也。
擬之而後言，議之而後動，擬議以成其變化。
與人同者，物必歸焉，故受之以大有。有大者不可以盈，故受之以謙。有大而能謙，必豫，故受之以豫。

書
帝曰：「來，禹！汝亦昌言。」禹拜曰：「都！帝，予何言？予思日孜孜。」
若虞機張，往省括于度，則釋。欽厥止，率乃祖攸行。
無總于貨寶，生生自庸，式敷民德，永肩一心。

First Session

Four Books
"Learn as if you could not reach your goal, and still fear losing what you have gained." [Analects 8.17]
"Therefore the administration of government lies in getting the proper men. Such men are to be got by means of the ruler's own character. That character is to be cultivated by his treading in the ways of duty. And the treading those ways of duty is to be cultivated by the cherishing of benevolence." [Doctrine of the Mean 20]
"Do not do what you would not otherwise do; do not desire what you would not otherwise desire. That is all." [Mencius 7A.17]

Classic of Changes (Yi)
"When the primal creative power of Qian uses the Nine, one sees the laws of Heaven." [Hexagram 1, Qian, Wenyan commentary]
"Nine in the fifth place: If in truth you have a kind heart, ask not—it is supremely auspicious. Truly, kindness will be recognized as my virtue. The Commentary on the Images says: 'If in truth you have a kind heart, ask not about it.' 'Kindness is recognized as my virtue': your aspiration is grandly fulfilled." [Hexagram 42, Yi]
"Consider it first and then speak; deliberate upon it first and then act. Through consideration and deliberation, one brings about transformations." [Xici shang 8]
"To one who enters into fellowship with others, things are certain to歸 (turn and belong); therefore Fellowship with Men is followed by Possession in Great Measure (Dayou). One who possesses in great measure must not allow himself to become full to overflowing; therefore it is followed by Modesty (Qian). One who possesses in great measure and yet is able to be modest is sure to enjoy enthusiasm and comfort; therefore it is followed by Enthusiasm (Yu)." [Xugua commentary]

Classic of Documents (Shu)
The Emperor said, "Come, Yu! Do you also make a splendid speech." Yu bowed and said, "Oh! Emperor, what can I say? I think only of being diligent day by day." [Yi and Ji]
"Be like the forester who, when the bow-trigger is drawn, goes to examine how the arrow-nock aligns with the rule, and only then releases it. Reverently rest in your proper place, and follow the path your ancestor walked." [Tai Jia shang]
"Do not amass goods and treasures, but employ yourself in fostering life upon life; thereby spread abroad virtue among the people, and forever bear a single mind." [Pan Geng xia]

translation_en:
…virtuous deeds in order to instruct the realm. The mind of the Two Sages is none other than the mind of Heaven and of Yao and Shun. Can the headings of the three books be enumerated in full? Can a general outline be given of the matters recorded therein? The Book of Documents says: "On him who does good, He sends down a hundred blessings." This is the natural response of the Way of Heaven. As you students recite and study the Sacred Instructions, you must surely strive after goodness, becoming loyal ministers and filial sons, and thereby be able to bring about blessings. Whom, indeed, will you take as your model? Or will you draw from them all comprehensively and carry it to the utmost? Each of you should state your views so that we may observe your aspirations.

Question: Confucius was the one who inherited the Way of the emperors and kings. What he taught to his own time and transmitted to later scholars ought to have no differences; yet there seem to be differences—let us discuss them together. Yao, Shun, and Yu held fast to the Mean (zhizhong), Tang established the Mean (jianzhong), and King Wu established the Supreme Standard (jianji); their governance was already flourishing. Yet when Confucius instructed Duke Ai, he said, "In all governance of the realm, the state, and the family, there are nine standard rules, and that by which they are practiced is one." And when Yan Yuan asked about governing a state, he said, "Follow the calendar of Xia, ride in the state carriage of Yin, wear the ceremonial cap of Zhou, and for music, take the Shao with its dance." Zengzi, Zisi, and Mencius were those who transmitted the Way of Confucius. Yet when Zengzi discussed bringing peace to the realm, it lay in the principle of the measuring square (xieju), as well as managing wealth and employing men; Zisi said, "In ruling the realm as a true king, there are three important things"; and when Mencius discussed the Kingly Way, he cited the well-field system and schools. Why do their doctrines differ? Could it be that practicing the Way in later times need not be the same as in antiquity? Is what Confucius called "one"…

可以承二帝三王否與抑固自有本末與若漢
唐宋之君其所行者亦有合於前之所謂者
與願聞至當之説
問古之治天下者必資輔相輔相之職當為上
為德為下為民今畧舉以為問漢之申屠
嘉衛綰田蚡公孫弘劉屈氂田千秋于定國
唐之蘇頲張九齡李泌楊綰陸贄裴垍李

===

與果有裨於上有益於下與世之論賢相
者曰蕭曹丙魏房杜姚宋韓范富歐若申
屠以下可與之並與抑或有過之者與諸生

問：古之治天下者，必資輔相。輔相之職，當為上為德，為下為民。今畧舉以為問：漢之申屠嘉、衛綰、田蚡、公孫弘、劉屈氂、田千秋、于定國，唐之蘇頲、張九齡、李泌、楊綰、陸贄、裴垍、李絳，宋之趙普、吕蒙正、張齊賢、李沆、寇準、王旦、丁謂，皆甞居是任，其所存、所行可得而詳與？果有裨於上、有益於下與？世之論賢相者，曰蕭曹、丙魏、房杜、姚宋、韓范、富歐，若申屠以下，可與之並與？抑或有過之者與？諸生有志於用，當取法何人與？夫尚友古人，則必論其世。願備言之，毋事退讓。

translation_en:
…indeed what is meant by the "Mean" (zhong) and the "Supreme Standard" (ji)? If one can truly put into practice all the things mentioned above, can one thereby succeed to the heritage of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, or not? Or do they inherently possess their own roots and branches? As for the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, did their actions also accord in some measure with what was spoken of above? I wish to hear the most fitting explanation.

Question: Those of antiquity who governed All Under Heaven necessarily relied upon assistant ministers (fuxiang). The duty of an assistant minister ought to be to promote virtue on behalf of the ruler above and to care for the people below. Let me now briefly cite examples to pose a question: Shentu Jia 申屠嘉, Wei Wan 衛綰, Tian Fen 田蚡, Gongsun Hong 公孫弘, Liu Quli 劉屈氂, Tian Qianqiu 田千秋, and Yu Dingguo 于定國 of the Han; Su Ting 蘇頲, Zhang Jiuling 張九齡, Li Mi 李泌, Yang Wan 楊綰, Lu Zhi 陸贄, Pei Ji 裴垍, and Li Jiang 李絳 of the Tang; and Zhao Pu 趙普, Lü Mengzheng 吕蒙正, Zhang Qixian 張齊賢, Li Hang 李沆, Kou Zhun 寇準, Wang Dan 王旦, and Ding Wei 丁謂 of the Song—all once held this office. Can what they cherished in mind and what they carried out in practice be recounted in detail? Did they truly bring benefit to the ruler above and advantage to the people below? When the world discusses worthy chief ministers, it speaks of Xiao [He] and Cao [Can], Bing [Ji] and Wei [Xiang], Fang [Xuanling] and Du [Ruhui], Yao [Chong] and Song [Jing], Han [Qi] and Fan [Zhongyan], and Fu [Bi] and Ouyang [Xiu]. As for Shentu [Jia] and those listed after him, can they be ranked alongside these men, or were there perhaps some among them who surpassed them? Since you students aspire to be employed in governance, whom ought you to take as your models? Now, to befriend the ancients, one must examine the ages in which they lived. I wish you to set this forth in full, without resorting to diffidence.

Question: Troops are used to defend the people, and what is crucial among them is horses; certainly troops must be drilled and inspected, and horses must be bred and reared, before they can be fully adequate for use. Therefore, in antiquity the hunts of the four seasons were all conducted during intervals in agricultural work in order to practice military affairs. The Han inherited the system of the Qin, not practicing military drills during three seasons of the year; yet [?] there were drills conducted…

於長安水南門、於洛陽郊東門、於平樂觀下者；唐則教射於顯德殿，講武於并州城北、於驪山之下者；宋嘗大閱於西郊及東郊及白石教塲者。其行於何時？施以何法？兵之強盛若何？《周官》校人掌王馬之政，圉師掌教圉人養馬，至漢、唐、宋皆設苑監，置官以司牧。其所處何地？所用何法？馬之蕃息若何？凡其訓兵養馬之政，有可以施於今者否？請具陳之。

問：刑以輔治，虞舜所不廢也。周公《立政》，謂可以長國，而周之歷年可考矣。漢、唐之法，始自簡而浸密，其後寬詔皆屢下。嘗聞漢除肉刑、定箠令，有輕大辟三十四事，又至八十一事者；唐省决杖、定贓估，終歲大辟有止二十四人或五十八人者，果何代與？若然，可謂仁矣，其效宜不異於周，而皆不若者，何與？豈各有其故與？抑所以祈天永命，真在於此，或他有其道與？虞、周、漢、唐法律之書，可得而知也，願聞其悉。
translation_en:
… at the Southern Water Gate of Chang'an, at the Eastern Suburban Gate of Luoyang, and beneath the Pingle Pavilion; in the Tang, there were instances of instructing archery at the Xiande Palace and practicing military drills north of the city wall of Bingzhou and at the foot of Mount Li; and the Song once held grand reviews in the western suburbs, the eastern suburbs, and at the Baishi Parade Ground. At what times were these carried out? By what methods were they implemented? And how strong and flourishing were their troops? In the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), the Commandant of the Royal Stables (Jiaoren) had charge of the administration of the king's horses, and the Master of the Grooms (Yushi) had charge of instructing the grooms in rearing horses; down to the Han, Tang, and Song, all established pasture directorates and appointed officials to supervise herding. In what places were they located? What methods did they employ? And how prolific was the breeding of their horses? Among all their policies for training troops and rearing horses, are there any that can be put into practice today? Please set them forth in full.

Question: Punishments as an aid to governance were not dispensed with even by Yu Shun. In the "Establishment of Government" (Lizheng), the Duke of Zhou said that through this one could perpetuate the state, and the longevity of the Zhou dynasty can be verified. The laws of the Han and Tang began in simplicity and gradually grew more intricate, after which edicts of leniency were repeatedly issued in both dynasties. We have heard that the Han abolished corporal mutilation and established ordinances on bastinado, and that there were instances of commuting capital offenses in thirty-four cases, and again in up to eighty-one cases; and that the Tang reduced the infliction of the heavy rod and fixed the valuation of illicit goods, so that in an entire year capital executions amounted to only twenty-four men or fifty-eight men—in what reigns did these actually occur? If this was so, they may well be called benevolent, and their results ought not to have differed from those of the Zhou; yet neither equaled it—why is this? Could it be that each had its own reasons? Or does the means of praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate truly lie in this, or is there another way? The legal texts of Yu, Zhou, Han, and Tang can be known; we wish to hear about them in full detail.

text:
蘊蓄而有得於中者今則猶當恐或失焉必也日無忘
其所有可也向也究夫事物細微之理有得於已者
今則猶當憂或忘焉必也月無忘其所能可也其猶
恐失之之心為何如哉得既能致其功既得又能慮
其失學而至於成也夫豈難哉抑又論之成湯聖君
也日新又新而聖敬日躋成王賢王也日就月將而
緝熈光明聖賢者百世之師也學者取法於是而篤
念孔子之訓有日進之功無日退之弊豈非善學也

惟能擴充其羞惡之心則自修之道不外是矣盖人
之為所不為欲所不欲者以其無禮義制之也苟能
制之以禮義則所為所欲無不合理君子之自脩外
此又豈有他道哉盖嘗論之為者指一身之動而言
也欲者指一念之動而言也為者動之著欲者動之
幾盖人於所不當為之事所不當欲之物初亦知之
至於私意一萌物欲牽引不能制之以禮義遂至於
為所不為者有焉欲所不欲者有焉苟能反是心以
擴充其羞惡之心於事至之時以義制之不為私意
===
之所蔽物来之際以禮制之不為物欲之所牽於是
所為者無不合其宜所欲者無不當於理推而充之
若火之始然泉之始達而義不可勝用矣君子所以
脩乎身者外此豈有他道哉抑嘗考之無為其所不
為是就躬行上克治所謂志士勵行守之於為也無
欲其所不欲是就心之發念處克治所謂哲人知幾
誠之於思也學者欲制乎身心而盡夫自脩之力豈
可舍是而他求哉

之爲所不爲欲所不欲者以其無禮義制之也苟能
制之以禮義則所爲所欲無不合理君子之自脩外
此又豈有他道哉盖嘗論之爲者指一身之動而言
也欲者指一念之動而言也爲者動之著欲者動之
幾盖人於所不當爲之事所不當欲之物初亦知之
至於私意一萌物欲牽引不能制之以禮義遂至於
爲所不爲者有焉欲所不欲者有焉苟能反是心以
擴充其羞惡之心於事至之時以義制之不爲私意
===
之所蔽物來之際以禮制之不爲物欲之所牽於是
所爲者無不合其宜所欲者無不當於理推而充之
若火之始然泉之始達而義不可勝用矣君子所以
脩乎身者外此豈有他道哉抑嘗考之無爲其所不
爲是就躬行上克治所謂志士勵行守之於爲也無
欲其所不欲是就心之發念處克治所謂哲人知幾
誠之於思也學者欲制乎身心而盡夫自脩之力豈
可舍是而他求哉
易
punctuated:
惟能擴充其羞惡之心，則自修之道不外是矣。盖人之為所不為、欲所不欲者，以其無禮義制之也。苟能制之以禮義，則所為所欲無不合理，君子之自脩，外此又豈有他道哉？盖嘗論之，為者，指一身之動而言也；欲者，指一念之動而言也。為者動之著，欲者動之幾。盖人於所不當為之事、所不當欲之物，初亦知之；至於私意一萌，物欲牽引，不能制之以禮義，遂至於為所不為者有焉，欲所不欲者有焉。苟能反是心以擴充其羞惡之心，於事至之時，以義制之，不為私意之所蔽；物来之際，以禮制之，不為物欲之所牽。於是所為者無不合其宜，所欲者無不當於理，推而充之，若火之始然、泉之始達，而義不可勝用矣。君子所以脩乎身者，外此豈有他道哉？抑嘗考之，「無為其所不為」，是就躬行上克治，所謂「志士勵行，守之於為」也；「無欲其所不欲」，是就心之發念處克治，所謂「哲人知幾，誠之於思」也。學者欲制乎身心而盡夫自脩之力，豈可舍是而他求哉？

易
translation_en:
Only when one is able to expand and develop one's mind of shame and dislike does the way of self-cultivation lie in nothing other than this. For the reason people do what they should not do and desire what they should not desire is that they lack propriety and righteousness to regulate themselves. If one can regulate oneself with propriety and righteousness, then whatever one does and whatever one desires will in every case accord with principle. Aside from this, how could there be any other way for the gentleman's self-cultivation?

To discuss this further: "doing" refers to the movement of the whole person, whereas "desiring" refers to the movement of a single thought. "Doing" is movement made manifest; "desiring" is the subtle incipient stir of movement. Now regarding matters that ought not to be done and things that ought not to be desired, people at first also know what they are. Yet once selfish intentions sprout and material desires pull them along, if they cannot regulate them with propriety and righteousness, they consequently reach the point where there are cases of doing what they should not do and cases of desiring what they should not desire. If one can turn this mind around so as to expand and develop one's mind of shame and dislike—when affairs arrive, regulating them with righteousness so as not to be obscured by selfish intentions, and when external things come, regulating them with propriety so as not to be dragged along by material desires—then whatever one does will in every case suit what is appropriate, and whatever one desires will in every case match principle. Extending and filling it out, it will be like a fire just beginning to burn or a spring just beginning to flow forth, and righteousness will be more than can ever be exhausted. Aside from this, how could there be any other way by which the gentleman cultivates his person?

Moreover, if we examine the matter: "Do not do what you would not do" is overcoming and governing oneself at the level of personal conduct—what is meant by "the man of high resolve refines his conduct and guards it in his actions." "Do not desire what you would not desire" is overcoming and governing oneself at the point where thoughts first arise in the mind—what is meant by "the wise man perceives the subtle incipient stirrings and makes himself sincere in his thoughts." If scholars wish to regulate body and mind and exert to the utmost their effort in self-cultivation, how could they set this aside and seek elsewhere?

Book of Changes (Yi)

translation_en:
"With one who seeks fellowship with men, things will certainly come to belong to him; hence this is followed by Great Possession (Dayou). One who possesses what is great must not allow himself to become full to overflowing; hence this is followed by Modesty (Qian). One who possesses what is great and yet can be modest will certainly know delight; hence this is followed by Delight (Yu)."
Yang Ding 楊鼎

Comment by Associate Examiner, Senior Compiler Zhong: Most writers in the examination compound were in the dark regarding this topic; this paper deeply grasps the Master's purport in ordering the hexagrams.
Comment by Examiner, Academician Lan: The moral principles of the Changes (Yi) are clear, and the language flows smoothly.
Comment by Examiner, Vice Minister Wang: This topic is fundamentally straightforward, yet people mostly overlook it, making good compositions hard to come by; only this essay is admirably fluent and clear.

Those who wish to observe the sequence of the hexagrams of the Changes ought to seek out the meaning behind the ordering of the hexagrams. For a hexagram must first possess its meaning before it is placed in sequence; if one merely observes their sequence without seeking out their meaning, how could one understand the sage's intention in ordering the hexagrams? Now, the hexagram with Qian above and Li below is Fellowship with Men (Tongren). Qian is heaven and Li is fire; their two natures tend in the same direction, and therefore it holds the meaning of fellowship with men. The hexagram with Li above and Qian below is Great Possession (Dayou). Fire high in the heavens illuminates every place without exception, and therefore it constitutes the meaning of great possession. Indeed, one who seeks fellowship with men is broad-minded, far-reaching, and free of selfishness, so those who turn to him in allegiance will inevitably be numerous—how could what he possesses fail to be great? It is for this reason that the sequence of the hexagrams makes Great Possession follow upon Fellowship with Men. As for the hexagram Modesty (Qian), its form is constituted by combining Kun and Gen: there is a mountain within the earth, which conveys the meaning of harboring height within lowliness. As for the hexagram Delight (Yu), its form is constituted by combining Zhen and Kun: thunder bursts forth from the earth, which conveys the meaning of unhindered flow and harmonious joy. Yet the reason Great Possession must be followed by Modesty is precisely that when what one possesses is already great, one easily reaches the point of fullness…

…fullness, therefore one ought to maintain it with Modesty (Qian), and thus be able to preserve what one possesses. That Modesty is necessarily followed by Enthusiasm (Yu) is likewise because when one possesses greatness and yet is capable of modesty, there is naturally peace, harmony, and joyful pleasure; therefore it is succeeded by Enthusiasm, which thus matches the virtue of Modesty. In ordering the hexagrams, our Master [Confucius] took their names and made manifest their meanings—how supreme was his intention in instructing people! Moreover, if we discuss it further: in the composition of the Ten Wings (Shi yi), the Great Images (Daxiang) already elucidated the hexagram lines of Fuxi, and the Commentary on the Judgments (Tuanzhuan) further elucidated the judgment words of King Wen; coming to the Words of the Text (Wenyan), the Appended Remarks (Xici), the Explanation of the Trigrams (Shuogua), and the Miscellaneous Hexagrams (Zagua), they further clarified the depths of their principles. Reaching this Sequence of the Hexagrams (Xugua), he further had to deduce and clarify the meaning of the sequence of the sixty-four hexagrams to serve as an exhortation and warning for the ways of the world—supreme indeed was the sage's heart of concern for the world! Those who do not know the Way claim that this is not the writing of the sage; how could they be worthy of discussing the Book of Changes (Yi)!

聖君明思導民於至善而継美乎前王正以民心從
教之易也夫善者民之所由以吉康者也乃其性之
本然而迪民以善者君道之當然也誠能法前代以
導民則民豈有不化哉此武王之自嚴畏因命康叔
故特舉以告之也其意盖曰民之生也氣稟好尚之
不齊偏陂反側之不一明而思之欲使之獲吉康奚
可無開導之方啓迪之道哉迪之以善所以致之於
===
吉康也仁義人心之至善也吾必迪斯民以仁義焉
孝弟人性之固有也吾必導斯民以孝弟焉然迪民
以善豈他求哉亦惟法諸古而已彼克寛克仁彰信
兆民殷先哲王固嘗以德而化民矣吾其以是德安
治乎民而必與之匹焉可也懋昭大德建中于民殷
先哲王固嘗以是德而教民矣吾其亦以是德康保
乎民而必與之等焉可也矧今之民同一至善之性
未有導之以善而不從者烏可不知所以導之哉均
此帝降之衷無有迪之以善而不化者烏可不知所

聖君明思導民於至善，而継美乎前王，正以民心從教之易也。夫善者，民之所由以吉康者也，乃其性之本然；而迪民以善者，君道之當然也。誠能法前代以導民，則民豈有不化哉？此武王之自嚴畏，因命康叔，故特舉以告之也。其意盖曰：民之生也，氣稟好尚之不齊，偏陂反側之不一，明而思之，欲使之獲吉康，奚可無開導之方、啓迪之道哉？迪之以善，所以致之於吉康也。仁義，人心之至善也，吾必迪斯民以仁義焉；孝弟，人性之固有也，吾必導斯民以孝弟焉。然迪民以善，豈他求哉？亦惟法諸古而已。彼克寛克仁，彰信兆民，殷先哲王固嘗以德而化民矣，吾其以是德安治乎民，而必與之匹焉可也；懋昭大德，建中于民，殷先哲王固嘗以是德而教民矣，吾其亦以是德康保乎民，而必與之等焉可也。矧今之民，同一至善之性，未有導之以善而不從者，烏可不知所以導之哉？均此帝降之衷，無有迪之以善而不化者，烏可不知所
translation_en:
Examiner and Vice Minister Wang commented: "Because this topic includes one extra final clause, writers found it difficult to phrase their essays. This piece grasps the essential meaning, and its prose is sufficient to bring it out."

The sage ruler clearly reflects on guiding the people toward the highest good and emulating the excellence of former kings, precisely because the hearts of the people so easily follow instruction. Now, goodness is that whereby the people attain auspiciousness and peace; it is the inherent nature of their being. And to guide the people with goodness is the natural duty of the ruler's Way. If one can truly model oneself on former eras in guiding the people, how could the people fail to be transformed? This was King Wu's own reverent caution, which, on the occasion of giving his charge to Kangshu, he specially raised to instruct him.

His meaning was essentially this: As the people are born, their稟 (material endowments) and preferences are not uniform, and their partialities, perversities, and instabilities are not the same. Clearly reflecting upon this, if one wishes to cause them to obtain auspiciousness and peace, how could one lack a method of instruction and a way of guidance? To guide them with goodness is the means to bring them to auspiciousness and peace. Benevolence and righteousness are the highest good of the human heart; I must guide these people with benevolence and righteousness. Filial piety and fraternal respect are inherent to human nature; I must lead these people with filial piety and fraternal respect.

Yet in guiding the people with goodness, why seek elsewhere? One need only model oneself upon antiquity. Able to be寬 (magnanimous) and able to be benevolent, manifesting trustworthiness to the myriad people—the former wise kings of Yin indeed once transformed the people through virtue; I ought to use this virtue to bring peace and order to the people, and must match myself with them. Diligently making bright their great virtue and establishing the standard of centrality among the people—the former wise kings of Yin indeed once instructed the people through this virtue; I ought also to use this virtue to pacify and protect the people, and must make myself equal to them.

How much more so since the people of today all share the same nature of highest goodness—there have never been any who, when led with goodness, did not follow; how could one not know the means…

text:
以迪之哉武王之自嚴畏如此其化民之心可謂至
矣大抵康誥一書以明德慎罰爲綱領不敢侮鰥寡
以下文王之明德慎罰也汝念哉以下欲康叔明德
也敬哉乃罰以下欲康叔慎罰也析而言之雖爲二
合而言之明德又慎罰之本故於此又欲以德用罰
也吁武王尚德不尚罰之心於此可見
詩
虞芮質厥成文王蹶厥生
章綸
===
同考試官侍講王批此卷七篇詞婉理明而此文王
一篇發明蹶厥生意思甚好可取
同考試官侍講邢批本因人歸於質成之日人便見
文王有興起之勢他卷皆不能發此作得之

考試官侍郎王批篇中說文王興起之勢原於人心之
歸非文王本意甚善甚善
因人心感化之誠動聖人興起之勢此可見其德之
盛也盖德者感人之本而勢之所由動也今虞芮來

「虞芮質厥成，文王蹶厥生。」

translation_en:
…how to instruct them? With King Wu holding himself in such strict reverence and awe, his heart set on transforming the people can truly be called the utmost. On the whole, the book Announcement to Kang (Kang gao) takes making bright one's virtue and being cautious in punishments as its guiding principles. From "did not dare to despise the widower and widow" onward is about King Wen's making bright his virtue and being cautious in punishments; from "Do you bear this in mind!" onward, he wishes Kangshu to make bright his virtue; from "Be reverent! In your punishments..." onward, he wishes Kangshu to be cautious in punishments. Analyzed separately, although they are two things, taken together, making bright one's virtue is in turn the root of being cautious in punishments; therefore, at this point he again wishes him to apply punishments by means of virtue. Ah! King Wu's heart that esteemed virtue rather than punishments can be seen right here.

Book of Odes (Shi)
"Yu and Rui brought their dispute to a settlement; King Wen stirred up his rising."
Zhang Lun 

Associate Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Wang comments: The seven essays of this scroll are gentle in diction and clear in principle, and this essay on King Wen brings out the meaning of "stirred up his rising" very well; it is worthy of selection.
Associate Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Xing comments: Originally, because people gave their allegiance on the day the dispute was brought to a settlement, people thereupon saw that King Wen possessed the momentum of rising up. None of the other scrolls were able to bring this out, whereas this composition has grasped it.
Examiner Academician Lan comments: The diction is warm and elegant, capturing the intent of the poet.
Examiner Vice Minister Wang comments: In the essay it says that the momentum of King Wen's rising up originated from the allegiance of people's hearts and was not King Wen's original intention—very good, very good!

title: 正統四年會試錄
text:
質其訟之成而文王由此動其興起之勢謂非本其
德之盛可乎昔者周公追述太王始遷岐周以開王業
而文王因之以受天命以戒成王謂夫虞芮二國之
爭田其不平也久矣一旦聞文王作興乃相與朝周
以質其訟之成焉及入其境則見耕夫行侣有遜讓之
俗入其朝則見卿士大夫有謙退之風二國之君感
而相讓遂以其田為閒田而退於是四十餘國聞之
而來歸三分天下以之而有二則文王興起之勢豈
不由此而動哉盖人心之歸即天命之歸也然文王
===
知事殷而已人見其氣勢則勃然而興起焉文王知
盡臣節而已人見其威靈則蹶然而動人焉四方以
之而無拂天下以之而有歸動其興起之勢如此非
其德之盛又何以感人心而致是哉是宜詩人形之
詠歌以賛美之也抑考是詩凡九章一章言太王在
邠二章言至岐三章言定宅四章言授田居民五章言
作宗廟六章言作宫室七章言作門社八章言至文
王而服昆夷九章遂言文王受命之事周公備述以
為成王告者盖欲知祖宗創業之艱難而今日守成

punctuated: 質其訟之成，而文王由此動其興起之勢，謂非本其德之盛，可乎？昔者周公追述太王始遷岐周以開王業，而文王因之以受天命，以戒成王。謂夫虞、芮二國之爭田，其不平也久矣。一旦聞文王作興，乃相與朝周，以質其訟之成焉。及入其境，則見耕夫行侣有遜讓之俗；入其朝，則見卿士大夫有謙退之風。二國之君，感而相讓，遂以其田為閒田而退。於是四十餘國聞之而來歸，三分天下以之而有二，則文王興起之勢，豈不由此而動哉？盖人心之歸，即天命之歸也。然文王知事殷而已，人見其氣勢則勃然而興起焉；文王知盡臣節而已，人見其威靈則蹶然而動人焉。四方以之而無拂，天下以之而有歸。動其興起之勢如此，非其德之盛，又何以感人心而致是哉？是宜詩人形之詠歌以賛美之也。抑考是詩凡九章：一章言太王在邠，二章言至岐，三章言定宅，四章言授田居民，五章言作宗廟，六章言作宫室，七章言作門社，八章言至文王而服昆夷，九章遂言文王受命之事。周公備述以為成王告者，盖欲知祖宗創業之艱難，而今日守成
translation_en: …to have their dispute settled, and from this King Wen set in motion the momentum of his rise; could one say that this was not rooted in the abundance of his virtue? In the past, the Duke of Zhou recounted how King Tai first moved to Qizhou to found the royal enterprise, and how King Wen built upon this to receive the Mandate of Heaven, so as to admonish King Cheng. He said that in the dispute over fields between the two states of Yu and Rui, their grievance had lasted a long time. Once they heard that King Wen had arisen, they went together to the court of Zhou to have their lawsuit settled. When they entered his borders, they saw that the plowmen and travelers had the custom of yielding to one another; when they entered his court, they saw that the ministers, officers, and grandees had the manner of modest deference. The rulers of the two states were moved and yielded to each other, and thereupon left the fields as unoccupied land and withdrew. At this, more than forty states heard of it and came in allegiance, so that thereby he held two-thirds of the realm; was not the momentum of King Wen's rise thus set in motion by this? For the allegiance of human hearts is none other than the allegiance of the Mandate of Heaven. Yet King Wen knew only to serve Yin, while others, seeing his vigor and momentum, saw him suddenly rise up; King Wen knew only to fulfill his integrity as a subject, while others, seeing his majesty and numinous power, saw him briskly stir men. Through this the four quarters offered no resistance, and through this the realm turned to him in allegiance. That the momentum of his rise was stirred like this—if not for the abundance of his virtue, how else could he have moved human hearts and brought this about? It was fitting indeed that the poet gave it form in song to praise and extol him. Moreover, if we examine this ode, it has nine stanzas in all: the first stanza speaks of King Tai being in Bin; the second stanza speaks of his arrival at Qi; the third stanza speaks of settling the dwellings; the fourth stanza speaks ofallotting fields and settling the people; the fifth stanza speaks of building the ancestral temple; the sixth stanza speaks of building the palace chambers; the seventh stanza speaks of building the gates and the altar of the soil; the eighth stanza speaks of how down to King Wen the Kunyi tribes were subdued; and the ninth stanza then speaks of the matter of King Wen receiving the Mandate. Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"The men of Qi made an incursion into our western borderlands." "The men of Qi attacked our northern borderlands." "The Duke, with the army of Chu, attacked Qi." [All from the twenty-sixth year of Duke Xi.] "The Marquis of Qi attacked our northern borderlands." "Jisun Xingfu, Zangsun Xu, Shusun Qiaoru, and Gongsun Yingqi led a force and met Xi Ke of Jin, Sun Liangfu of Wei, and Prince Shou of Cao, and fought a battle with the Marquis of Qi at An." [Both from the second year of Duke Cheng.] "The army of Qi attacked our northern borderlands." "The Duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Little Zhu in jointly besieging Qi." [Both from the eighteenth year of Duke Xiang.] "Guo Xia of Qi led a force and attacked our western borderlands." [Seventh year of Duke Ding.] "The Duke made an incursion into Qi." [Eighth year of Duke Ding.] "The Duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu." [Tenth year of Duke Ding.]

Qian Pu 錢溥

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Surveillance Commissioner Hua 花: The Spring and Autumn Annals esteems virtue and does not esteem force. This paper perceives that Lu's relying on military force to avenge the grievances against the men of Qi was not as good as winning over the hearts of the men of Qi through the transforming influence of the Sage. It accords precisely with the purport of the Classic and deserves to be placed among the selected ranks.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Left Administrator Jin 金: The two states engaged in warfare for generation after generation, yet in a single morning submitted to the transforming influence of the Sage. This composition rises and falls in tone with incisive force, deeply grasping the meaning of the topic. At the end, where it speaks of transforming Qi and transforming Lu, it is so evocative as to draw repeated sighs of admiration—most delightful indeed! It ought to be singled out and published.

Comment by Examiner and Academician Lan 蘭: Its diction is stern and its principles upright; its praise and blame are fittingly measured. This is someone thoroughly versed in this Classic.

太公周公之子孫僖公之世孝公以洮向二盟致憾於
===
魯今日侵我西鄙明日伐我北鄙是陵弱之師也魯
不能持國以自防乃乞師于楚以致伐資夷狄以取
其邑焉成公之日齊頃有叛伯之謀又為伐魯之舉
是亦不義之師也魯乗列卿之憤怒遂為于鞌之大
戰恃伯力以覆其師焉迨齊環棄好伐我北鄙我公
既嘗會列國以同討景公爭伯伐我北鄙我公又嘗

When troubles repeatedly arise and weapons clash with a powerful state, it is not worthy of praise; when ritual propriety is specially cultivated and moral transformation extends to a powerful state, it is cause for delight. In the days of Duke Cheng of Lu, Duke Qing of Qi plotted to turn against the hegemon and again undertook an expedition against Lu—this too was an unrighteous army. Riding on the indignation of the ranking ministers of the feudal states, Lu then fought the great battle at An, relying on the hegemon's strength to overthrow Qi's army.

息則久久則徵徵則悠遠悠遠則博厚博厚則高明
者此誠也天與聖人豈有二理哉孔子繫易則曰易
有太極周子太極圖則曰無極而太極而通書又曰

也太極靜而生陰乾道變化各正性命者誠之立也
此則一陰一陽之謂道非誠爲之本乎自聖人論之
其氣禀粹然其德性渾然所以然者亦以誠爲之本
焉誠者何亦真實無妄之謂也即所謂太極也聖人
本是誠而動也即陽之建而仁禮之理具焉仁則均
其所愛禮則嘉其所會蓋與天之元亨同一機聖人
本是誠而靜也即陰之順而義智之理具焉義則足
以利物智則足以幹事與天之利貞同一致是則聖
人定之以仁義中正而主靜又非誠爲之本乎由是
===
論之則知天有太極者誠也聖人立人極者亦誠也
天自太極而陰陽而五行四時自古至今無一息之

punctuated: 也。太極靜而生陰，乾道變化，各正性命者，誠之立也。此則一陰一陽之謂道，非誠為之本乎？自聖人論之，其氣稟粹然，其德性渾然，所以然者，亦以誠為之本焉。誠者何？亦真實無妄之謂也，即所謂太極也。聖人本是誠而動也，即陽之健，而仁禮之理具焉。仁則均其所愛，禮則嘉其所會，盖與天之元亨同一機。聖人本是誠而靜也，即陰之順，而義智之理具焉。義則足以利物，智則足以幹事，與天之利貞同一致。是則聖人定之以仁義中正而主靜，又非誠為之本乎？由是論之，則知天有太極者，誠也；聖人立人極者，亦誠也。天自太極而陰陽，而五行四時，自古至今，無一息之停，所謂「渾兮闢兮，其無窮兮」者，此誠也。聖人自一心而健順，而五常百行，自始至終，無一息之間，所謂「不息則久，久則徵，徵則悠遠，悠遠則博厚，博厚則高明」者，此誠也。天與聖人豈有二理哉？孔子繫易則曰：「易有太極。」周子太極圖則曰：「無極而太極。」而通書又曰：「誠者，聖人之本。」盖太極即誠，論天即聖人也。大哉誠乎！其天與聖人之本體乎！是為論。
translation_en: …is so. When the Supreme Ultimate is still, it generates yin; that “the Way of Qian transforms and changes, and each thing receives its proper nature and destiny” is the establishment of sincerity. This is what is meant by “one yin and one yang are called the Way.” Is sincerity not its foundation? Speaking of the sage, his endowment of vital energy is pure, and his moral nature is whole. These, too, have sincerity as their foundation. What is sincerity? It likewise means being real and true, without falsity: it is what is called the Supreme Ultimate. When the sage acts on the basis of this sincerity, his activity is the vigor of yang, and the principles of benevolence and ritual propriety are fully present within it. Through benevolence he extends his love impartially; through ritual propriety he brings excellence to what he gathers together. These share a single working with Heaven’s origination and flourishing. When the sage is still on the basis of this sincerity, his stillness is the yielding of yin, and the principles of righteousness and wisdom are fully present within it. Righteousness suffices to benefit things, and wisdom suffices to manage affairs. These accord wholly with Heaven’s benefiting and constancy. Thus the sage establishes the standard through benevolence, righteousness, centrality, and correctness, taking stillness as primary. Does this not also have sincerity as its foundation? Reasoning from this, we know that sincerity accounts for Heaven’s possession of the Supreme Ultimate, and sincerity likewise accounts for the sage’s establishment of the Ultimate of Humanity. Heaven proceeds from the Supreme Ultimate to yin and yang, and thence to the Five Phases and four seasons, without pausing for a single breath from antiquity to the present. What is described as “undivided, then opening out, inexhaustibly” is this sincerity. The sage proceeds from his single mind to vigor and yielding, and thence to the five constant virtues and the hundred forms of conduct, without a single breath’s interruption from beginning to end. What is described as “unceasing, and therefore enduring; enduring, and therefore manifest; manifest, and therefore far-reaching; far-reaching, and therefore broad and substantial; broad and substantial, and therefore lofty and luminous” is this sincerity. Could Heaven and the sage have two different principles? In his Appended Statements to the Changes, Kongzi says: “The Changes has the Supreme Ultimate.” In his Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate, Master Zhou says: “Without ultimate, yet the Supreme Ultimate.” His Comprehensive Writings (Tongshu) further says: “Sincerity is the foundation of the sage.” The Supreme Ultimate is indeed sincerity; to discuss Heaven is to discuss the sage. Great indeed is sincerity! Is it not the fundamental substance of Heaven and the sage? This concludes the discourse.

Whenever there is the sage of an era, there must be the supreme governance of that era; whenever there is the supreme governance of an era, there must be the canonical statutes of that era. The three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) by Our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), and the two books Secret Merits of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and True Exemplars of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) by the Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen (Taizong, the Yongle Emperor)—are these not the very canonical statutes of supreme governance? Whenever I humbly read the books of the Two Sages, I never fail to bow my head to my hands and touch my forehead to the ground, proclaiming aloud: "Great indeed are the Imperial words! Unified indeed is the Imperial mind!" Truly, they serve to establish the mind for Heaven and Earth, to establish the destiny for the living people, to carry on the governance of past sages, and to bestow blessings upon this world.

The three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements comprise over two hundred articles in total. Although the matters recorded in them are varied, the good examples can inspire people's good hearts, while the evil ones can chastise and restrain people's wayward wills. This is the intention of encouraging the world, molding customs, promoting good, and stopping evil. Secret Merits of Doing Good records one hundred and fifty-six individuals, headed by Jiang Ziwen (蔣子文); although there is a distinction between the unseen and the manifest realms, none of it is anything other than teaching people to do good. True Exemplars of Filial Piety records two hundred and seven individuals, headed by Yu Shun (虞舜); although there are differences between adversity and eminence, none of it is anything other than teaching people to be filial.

The mind of the Two Sages is none other than the mind of the Way of Heaven in blessing the good and bringing misfortune upon the wicked, and the mind of Yao and Shun in showing benevolence to the people and cherishing all things. …are all this. As for the governance of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, none ever came close to this, which is why they remain open to criticism. Allow me to follow Your enlightened question and reply with a ten-thousandth part of the matter.

Once the royal chariot tracks of the Zhou moved east, no sovereign of the Supreme Standard arose, and the Way of the Emperors and Kings ceased to be transmitted. Heaven gave birth to Confucius, who exerted his strength to rouse and revive it. What he preserved within was the mind of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu; what he inherited was the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu. Therefore, in what he instructed his contemporaries and transmitted to later scholars, though the words seemed different, their substance was the same. Now, "sincerely hold fast the Mean" (yun zhi jue zhong) was what Yao imparted to Shun, and what Shun imparted to Yu. When Yu transmitted this to Tang, it was called "establishing the Mean among the people" (jian zhong yu min); when Tang transmitted this to King Wu, it was called "the Sovereign establishing his Supreme Standard" (huang jian qi you ji). The efficacy of their attainment of order reached the highest flourishing in every case.

Although Confucius did not obtain a ruling position to put his Way into practice, one may know it by observing his teachings and instructions. When he told Duke Ai of the Nine Standard Rules (jiu jing), he placed cultivating the person first, for cultivating the person is the means to embody the Mean. When he told Yan Yuan of the rites and music of the Four Dynasties, it was a matter of deliberating and employing the Mean among them. At that time, the one who saw and knew it was Zengzi; Zengzi transmitted it to Zisi, and Zisi transmitted it to Mencius—all of it being the Way of Confucius. When Zengzi discussed bringing peace to the world, he located it in the "measuring square" (xieju), which means measuring by the natural principle of the one mind so as to seek conformity with the Mean. Zisi composed the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), saying: "In ruling the world there are three important things," meaning that in deliberating on rites, fixing regulations, and examining the written characters, one wishes them not to transgress the single Mean. Coming to Mencius's discussion of the Kingly Way, he raised the doctrines of the schools and the well-field system of the Three Dynasties: taxing one-tenth was regulating the Mean; [the teaching] of clarifying human relationships…

If one takes this up and puts it into practice, it will truly yield the exact same result as the Two Emperors and Three Kings. From that era downward, those dynasties renowned for good governance are merely the Han, the Tang, and the Song. This is why the office of Chief Minister is of such great weight. Before the Three Dynasties, those of the caliber of Gao Yao, Kui, Hou Ji, and Xie, and the peers of Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao, are beyond any need for discussion. From the Three Dynasties onward, however, their successes and failures, merits and demerits, can be examined. In the Han dynasty, Shentu Jia 申屠嘉, Wei Wan 衞綰, Gongsun Hong 公孫弘, Tian Fen 田蚡, Liu Quli 劉屈氂, Tian Qianqiu 田千秋, and Yu Dingguo 于定國 all served their sovereigns with poise in the imperial court. Yet it was Shentu Jia who curbed and suppressed favored minions and clarified the righteous duty between ruler and minister; it was Tian Qianqiu who, being generous, sincere, and wise, restored the affection between father and son. Between one who was humble, respectful, and courteous [Yu Dingguo] and one who twisted his learning to flatter the age and thus incurred the rebuke of Yuan Gu 轅固 [Gongsun Hong], which was superior? Between one who maintained himself with pure caution [Wei Wan] and one who was arrogant, extravagant, and destructive of righteousness so as to provoke the disdain of Ji An 汲黯 [Tian Fen], which again was better? As for one who consorted with imperial in-laws inside the court and allied with feudatory princes outside, thereby bringing disaster and ruin upon himself [Liu Quli], there was such a person as well. What they harbored in their minds and what they practiced in their actions can generally be seen. In the Tang dynasty, Su Ting 蘇頲, Zhang Jiuling 張九齡, Li Mi 李泌, Yang Wan 楊綰, Lu Zhi 陸贄, Pei Ji 裴垍, and Li Jiang 李絳 were all able to fulfill their responsibilities in serving their sovereigns and bring about good governance. Yet it was Su Ting who proposed what was acceptable and rejected what was objectionable, admonishing his sovereign with rectitude; it was Zhang Jiuling who was upright, firm, and square, guiding his sovereign onto the Way. Li Mi was earnestly devoted to the cardinal guides and constant virtues, while Lu Zhi was deeply committed to benevolence and righteousness. As for transforming others through pure frugality, none equaled Yang Wan; in offering frank and outspoken remonstrance, none equaled Li Jiang; and it was Pei Ji who was loyal in serving his sovereign and urged him to rectify his mind as the foundation for achieving order. What they harbored in their minds and what they practiced in their actions can once again be seen. 自持慊慨有大畧以皇王之道致君者張齊賢
也忠良純厚以進賢退不肖爲務者李沆也寇
準之兼資忠義秉道疾邪王旦之深沉德望明
識國體皆可謂賢矣惜旹進冊誤之言旦從天
書之僞皆是以累君德而丁謂之姦邪不可與
此例論也昔之論賢相者率曰蕭曹丙魏房杜
姚宋韓范富歐以愚觀之若漢申屠嘉及唐宋
諸公可與之並者蓋多其不足齒者蓋少矣而
先儒胡致堂嘗以陸贄爲天民程子又謂我朝

自持；慷慨有大畧，以皇王之道致君者，張齊賢也；忠良純厚，以進賢退不肖為務者，李沆也。寇準之兼資忠義，秉道疾邪；王旦之深沉德望，明識國體，皆可謂賢矣。惜準日進再誤之言，旦從天書之偽，皆足以累君德；而丁謂之姦邪，不可與此例論也。昔之論賢相者，率曰蕭、曹、丙、魏、房、杜、姚、宋、韓、范、富、歐。以愚觀之，若漢申屠嘉及唐、宋諸公，可與之並者盖多，其不足齒者盖少矣。而先儒胡致堂嘗以陸贄為天民，程子又謂我朝宰相當以李沆為第一，范文正公亦謂寇萊公為大忠，王文正公為大雅。愚之所取法者，當以先正之言為準；若等而上之，又當志伊尹之志而後可。請以是復明問。

… conducted himself [by the Right Way]; Zhang Qixian 張齊賢 was generous and possessed grand strategies, guiding his sovereign by the Way of the August Emperors and True Kings; and Li Hang 李沆 was loyal, virtuous, pure, and generous, making the promotion of the worthy and the dismissal of the unworthy his priority. Kou Zhun 寇準 combined loyalty and righteousness in his nature, upholding the Way and detesting wickedness; Wang Dan 王旦 possessed profound moral prestige and clearly understood the essentials of governance—both may be called worthy. Regrettably, Kou Zhun later offered the counsel that "[the realm] cannot be wronged a second time," and Wang Dan went along with the fabrication of the "Heavenly Texts," both of which were enough to blemish their sovereign's virtue; as for the treachery and wickedness of Ding Wei 丁謂, he cannot even be discussed in the same category as these men. Those in the past who discussed worthy chief councilors generally spoke of Xiao [He 蕭何] and Cao [Can 曹參], Bing [Ji 丙吉] and Wei [Xiang 魏相], Fang [Xuanling 房玄齡] and Du [Ruhui 杜如晦], Yao [Chong 姚崇] and Song [Jing 宋璟], and Han [Qi 韓琦], Fan [Zhongyan 范仲淹], Fu [Bi 富弼], and Ouyang [Xiu 歐陽修]. In my humble view, among men such as Shentu Jia 申屠嘉 of the Han and the various gentlemen of the Tang and Song mentioned above, those who can be ranked alongside them are indeed many, while those unworthy of mention are few. Moreover, the former Confucian scholar Hu Zhitang 胡致堂 [Hu Yin 胡寅] once regarded Lu Zhi 陸贄 as one of "Heaven's people" (tianmin); Master Cheng 程子 also said that among the chief councilors of his dynasty, Li Hang should be ranked first; and Duke Wenzheng of Fan (Fan Zhongyan) likewise called Duke Lai of Kou (Kou Zhun) a model of "great loyalty" and Duke Wenzheng of Wang (Wang Dan) a model of "great refinement." In choosing whom to take as models, I should take the words of these former worthies as my standard; and if one ascends a step higher still, only by setting one's aspiration upon the aspiration of Yi Yin 伊尹 will it suffice. I beg to offer this in reply to Your brilliant question.

養馬在敬與誠可謂知本之論
兵所以衛民非兵無以安民生馬所以資兵非馬
無以足兵用然非教閱之有道畜養之有方而
欲立武以强國盖難矣是故司馬之法春振旅
遂以蒐夏茇舍遂以苗秋治兵遂以獮冬大閱
遂以狩皆於農隙講武事也漢承秦制兵有三
時之休而行一時之講西漢每以歲十月會五

宗則講於幷州玄宗又講於驪山之下宋太宗
大閱于西郊真宗又閱於東郊至孝宗時則閱
於白石教塲其講閱也皆於農隙之時習夫坐
作擊刺之法振其精銳果敢之氣而得有以備

兵所以衛民，非兵無以安民生；馬所以資兵，非馬無以足兵用。然非教閱之有道、畜養之有方，而欲立武以强國，盖難矣。是故《司馬》之法：春振旅，遂以蒐；夏茇舍，遂以苗；秋治兵，遂以獮；冬大閱，遂以狩。皆於農隙講武事也。漢承秦制，兵有三時之休，而行一時之講。西漢每以歲十月，會五營士，講於長安水南門；至東漢，則以立秋日，講於洛陽郊東門；靈帝之時，詔發四方兵，講肄於平樂觀。唐太宗嘗選衛士，教射於顯德殿矣；高宗則講於幷州；玄宗又講於驪山之下。宋太宗大閱于西郊；真宗又閱於東郊；至孝宗時，則閱於白石教塲。其講閱也，皆於農隙之時，習夫坐作、擊刺之法，振其精銳、果敢之氣，而得有以備夫折衝、禦侮之用也。漢、唐、宋之教閱如此，兵豈有不强盛者哉？若夫《周官》，校人掌五馬：曰種馬，曰戎馬，曰齊馬，曰田馬，曰駑馬；圉師掌六閑之…

Examiner and Vice Minister Wang comments: "All five policy essays are well-answered, and this one is the most outstanding among them. At the end of the essay, it states that training troops and breeding horses depend on reverence and sincerity; this can truly be called an argument that understands the fundamentals."

Troops are the means by which the people are protected; without troops, there is no way to secure the people's livelihood. Horses are the means by which troops are supported; without horses, there is no way to suffice for military use. Yet unless training and review follow the proper way, and breeding and rearing have the proper method, desiring to establish military might in order to strengthen the state is indeed difficult. Therefore, according to the laws of the Minister of War (Sima): in spring they marshal the troops and thereupon conduct the spring hunt (sou); in summer they make rustic encampments and thereupon conduct the summer hunt (miao); in autumn they drill the troops and thereupon conduct the autumn hunt (xian); in winter they hold the grand review and thereupon conduct the winter hunt (shou). All of these were to practice military affairs during the intervals of farming. The Han inherited the Qin system: the troops had rest during three seasons and carried out drills during one season. In the Western Han, every year in the tenth month, they assembled the soldiers of the Five Camps to drill at the Southern Water Gate of Chang'an. By the Eastern Han, on the day of the Beginning of Autumn, they drilled at the Eastern Suburb Gate of Luoyang; in the time of Emperor Ling, an imperial edict mobilized troops from the four quarters to drill and practice at the Pingle Lodge. Emperor Taizong of the Tang once selected imperial guards and taught them archery at the Xiande Palace; Gaozong drilled them in Bingzhou; Xuanzong also drilled them at the foot of Mount Li. Emperor Taizong of the Song held a grand review in the western suburbs; Zhenzong also held a review in the eastern suburbs; and by the time of Xiaozong, he held a review at the Baishi Parade Ground. In their drilling and reviewing, they always used the intervals of farming to practice the methods of sitting and rising, striking and thrusting, rousing their spirit of elite sharpness and resolute daring, so as to be prepared for the use of repelling enemy assaults and warding off aggression. With the training and reviews of the Han, Tang, and Song being such as this, how could their troops not be strong and flourishing? As for the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), the Director of Horse Pastures (Jiaoren) was in charge of five kinds of horses: stud horses, war horses, ceremonial horses, hunting horses, and inferior horses; the Master of Grooms (Yushi) was in charge of the [instruction] of the six corrals…

教，圉人掌養馬之事，其制甚善。逮秦開阡陌、廢井田，馬政亦以之而廢。漢初稍復古制，勸民養馬於內郡，復縱民畜牧于邊塞，其後遂設三十六苑，分置西北邊，牧馬至三十萬匹。唐收戰伐餘馬，自赤岸澤徙之隴右，命張萬歲為太僕，自貞觀訖於麟德，馬至七十餘萬匹。開元初，王毛仲為內外閑廄使，牧養有法，盛比麟德。宋畜於監牧者曰官馬，散於編戸者曰戸馬，市於邊郡者曰戎馬。內設騏驥院、天駟監、天廄坊，又制羣牧使；外自河北至許州，置監凡一十有八，兩河、陝西、太原、交城亦各有監，總以羣牧，而守倅得兼領焉，所養亦至十餘萬匹。此歷代之馬政然也。然而始之立法非不善也，久則不能無弊焉，於是而有耗焉。蓋馬盛則兵彊，兵彊則國威以振，豈可不加之意哉！

… training, and the Grooms (yuren) had charge of the tasks of rearing horses; this system was most excellent. When Qin opened up the field paths and abolished the well-field system, horse administration was consequently abolished along with it. At the beginning of the Han dynasty, the ancient system was gradually restored: the people were encouraged to rear horses in the interior commanderies, and were again permitted to pasture livestock freely along the frontier passes. Thereafter, thirty-six pasturages were established and distributed along the northwestern frontier, where pastured horses reached three hundred thousand head. The Tang gathered the horses remaining from military campaigns and moved them from Chi'an Marsh (Chi'anze) to Longyou, appointing Zhang Wansui 張萬歲 as Chamberlain for the Imperial Stud (Taipu). From the Zhenguan (627–649) to the Linde (664–665) eras, the horses reached more than seven hundred thousand head. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era (713–741), Wang Maozhong 王毛仲 served as Commissioner of the Palace and Imperial Corrals and Stables (Neiwai xianjiu shi); his pasturing and rearing followed proper methods, and the abundance rivaled that of the Linde era. In the Song, those reared in the Directorate Pasturages were called "official horses" (guanma), those distributed among registered households were called "household horses" (huma), and those purchased in frontier commanderies were called "military horses" (rongma). In the capital, they established the Fine Steeds Institute (Qiji yuan), the Directorate of Celestial Steeds (Tiansi jian), and the Celestial Stables Service (Tianjiu fang), and also instituted the Herd Office Commissioners (Qunmu shi). In the provinces, from Hebei to Xuzhou, they established eighteen directorates in all, while Lianghe, Shaanxi, Taiyuan, and Jiaocheng each had their own directorates as well; these were overseen overall by the Herd Offices, with prefects and vice prefects permitted to hold concurrent charge of them, and the horses reared also reached more than one hundred thousand head. Such was the horse administration of successive dynasties. Yet it was not that the laws established at the outset were not good; after a long time they could not be free of abuses, and consequently wastage and depletion arose. Indeed, when horses are abundant, the army is strong; when the army is strong, the prestige of the state is thereby roused—how could one not pay close attention to this?

Reverently reflecting upon our dynasty, the successive Sacred Emperors have inherited the line one from another, dedicating their energies to good governance; in their methods for training troops and rearing horses, they have achieved utter perfection and excellence. Inside the capital there are the Imperial Bodyguard (Qinjun) as well as the Headquarters of the Supreme Commanders (Zongrong zhi fu), while outside in the provinces, large and small military guards are arrayed like pieces on a chessboard and stars in the sky; they are drilled and reviewed according to the seasons, so the troops are elite and sharp. Inside the capital there is the Court of the Imperial Stud (Taipu), while outside in the provinces there are established the Branch Courts of the Imperial Stud (Xing Taipu)…

子行將敷對大廷，以膺顯擢，當思爲上爲德，爲下爲民，以翼太平之盛。若徒以此爲仕進之階，甚或恣意於富貴利達，盡棄平昔之所學，則非朝廷選賢命士之意矣。尚勗之哉！
行在翰林院學士臣藺從善謹序。
translation_en:
…are soon to present their responses in the great court and receive illustrious appointments. They ought to reflect on practicing virtue for the sovereign above and caring for the people below, so as to assist the flourishing age of Great Peace. If they merely regard this as a stepping-stone to official advancement, or even give free rein to their desires for wealth, rank, profit, and prominence, completely abandoning what they have learned throughout their lives, then this would not be the Court's intention in selecting the worthy and commissioning scholars. May they strive earnestly!

Respectfully prefaced by your servant Lin Congshan 藺從善, Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy in the Auxiliary Administration.
